hmmt-feb-2001-calc-01.title: Length of each path
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-01.body:
A semicircle of radius $\frac1n$ has length $\pi\cdot\frac1n$. There are $n$ of them, so $L_n=n\cdot\frac\pi n=\pi$ for every $n$, and the limit is $\pi$.

**Answer: $\pi$**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-02.title: Find the critical and inflection points
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-02.body:
Let $f(x)=3x^5-250x^3+735x$. Then $f'(x)=15x^4-750x^2+735=15(x^2-1)(x^2-49)$, which changes sign at $x=\pm1,\pm7$: these are the four relative extrema. And $f''(x)=60x^3-1500x=60x(x^2-25)$ changes sign at $x=0,\pm5$: the three inflection points.

The $x$-coordinates are $\pm1,\pm7,0,\pm5$, which cancel in pairs, so their sum is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-03.title: Differentiate the volume
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-03.body:
Surface area $6s^2=6t$ gives edge $s=\sqrt t$, so the volume is $V=s^3=t^{3/2}$ and $\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac32\sqrt t$. When $6t=144$, $t=24$ and $\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac32\sqrt{24}=\frac32\cdot2\sqrt6=3\sqrt6$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt6$**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-04.title: Calculus
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-04.body:
Put the legs along the axes, $4$ on the $x$-axis and $3$ on the $y$-axis; the hypotenuse is $y=3-\frac34x$. A largest rectangle has a vertex at the right angle and the opposite vertex $(x,y)$ on the hypotenuse, with area $A(x)=x\left(3-\frac34x\right)=3x-\frac34x^2$. $A'(x)=3-\frac32x=0$ gives $x=2$ and $A=6-3=3$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-04.title: AM-GM
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-04.body:
With the opposite vertex $(x,y)$ on the hypotenuse, $\frac x4+\frac y3=1$. Then $\frac{xy}{12}=\frac x4\cdot\frac y3\le\left(\frac12\cdot1\right)^2=\frac14$, so $xy\le3$, with equality at $x=2,y=\frac32$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-05.title: Rectangle in terms of its height
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-05.body:
The hypotenuse is $5$ and the altitude onto it is $h=\frac{3\cdot4}{5}=\frac{12}5$. A rectangle with a side on the hypotenuse and height $y$ has width $5\left(1-\frac yh\right)$ (the cross-section at height $y$ of the triangle, which shrinks linearly). Its area is $A(y)=5y\left(1-\frac yh\right)$, a downward parabola with maximum at $y=\frac h2$: $A=5\cdot\frac h2\cdot\frac12=\frac{5h}{4}=3$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-06.title: Slope condition
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-06.body:
Differentiating, $2x-2(y-1)y'=0$, so the slope at $(a,b)$ is $\frac{a}{b-1}$. The tangent passes through the origin, so this slope equals $\frac ba$: $a^2=b(b-1)$. Together with $a^2-(b-1)^2=1$: $b^2-b-(b-1)^2=1$, so $b=2$, $a^2=2$, $a=\sqrt2$ (positive slope). Then $\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=\frac\pi4$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi4$**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-07.title: Partial fractions
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-07.body:
$1-3x+2x^2=(1-x)(1-2x)$ and $\dfrac1{(1-x)(1-2x)}=\dfrac2{1-2x}-\dfrac1{1-x}$ (check at $x=0$: $2-1=1$). Expanding as geometric series, the coefficient of $x^n$ is $2\cdot2^n-1=2^{n+1}-1$. For $n=12$: $2^{13}-1=8191$.

**Answer: 8191**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-07.title: Recurrence
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-07.body:
Let $c_n$ be the coefficient. From $(1-3x+2x^2)\sum c_nx^n=1$: $c_0=1$, $c_1=3$ and $c_n=3c_{n-1}-2c_{n-2}$. This gives $1,3,7,15,\dots$, i.e. $c_n=2^{n+1}-1$, so $c_{12}=8191$.

**Answer: 8191**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-08.title: Telescoping arctangents
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-08.body:
$\cot^{-1}(n^2+n+1)=\arctan\dfrac1{n^2+n+1}=\arctan\dfrac{(n+1)-n}{1+n(n+1)}=\arctan(n+1)-\arctan n$ by the tangent subtraction formula. The partial sum up to $N$ is $\arctan(N+1)-\arctan0=\arctan(N+1)\to\frac\pi2$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi2$**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-09.title: Solve the linear system
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-09.body:
The Kr that decays becomes Pl, and Pl decays at rate $2y$, so $x'=-x$, $y'=x-2y$ with $x(0)=10$, $y(0)=0$. Then $x=10e^{-t}$ and $y'+2y=10e^{-t}$. Multiplying by $e^{2t}$: $(ye^{2t})'=10e^{t}$, so $ye^{2t}=10e^t+C$, and $y(0)=0$ gives $C=-10$: $y=10\left(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\right)$.

$y'=10\left(-e^{-t}+2e^{-2t}\right)=0\iff e^{t}=2$, i.e. $t=\ln2$. This is a maximum, since $y'>0$ before and $y'<0$ after.

**Answer: $\ln2$**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-09.title: Use $y'=0$ directly
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-09.body:
$y$ is largest when $y'=0$, i.e. $x=2y$. With $x=10e^{-t}$ and $y=10(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})$ the condition is $e^{-t}=2e^{-t}-2e^{-2t}$, i.e. $e^{-t}=2e^{-2t}$, so $e^t=2$ and $t=\ln2$.

**Answer: $\ln2$**

hmmt-feb-2001-calc-10.title: Odd part vanishes; substitute $v=u^{333}$
hmmt-feb-2001-calc-10.body:
The term $\dfrac{4u^{1664}\sin u^{691}}{1+u^{666}}$ is odd in $u$ ($u^{1664}$ and $u^{666}$ are even, $\sin u^{691}$ is odd), so its integral over $[-1,1]$ is $0$.

For the rest, let $v=u^{333}$, so $dv=333u^{332}du$ and $u^{666}=v^2$, $u^{998}=u^{332}v^2$. Then
$$\int_{-1}^1\frac{2u^{332}+u^{998}}{1+u^{666}}du=\frac1{333}\int_{-1}^1\frac{2+v^2}{1+v^2}dv=\frac1{333}\int_{-1}^1\left(1+\frac1{1+v^2}\right)dv=\frac{2}{333}\left(1+\frac\pi4\right).$$
This equals $\dfrac{4+\pi}{666}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{2}{333}\left(1+\dfrac\pi4\right)=\dfrac{4+\pi}{666}$**
